content: Tsuga, commonly known as hemlock, is a genus of coniferous trees belonging to the family Pinaceae. The name hemlock originates from the resemblance of the crushed foliage's scent to that of the unrelated herb poison hemlock. However, unlike the herb, Tsuga species are not toxic. The genus comprises between eight and ten species, depending on the taxonomic authority, with four species native to North America and four to six species found in eastern Asia. Tsuga trees are medium to large evergreen conifers, typically growing to heights of 20–60 meters, with some species reaching up to 79 meters. They exhibit a conical to irregular crown, with irregular forms more common in certain Asian species. The leading shoots of these trees often droop. The bark is scaly, deeply furrowed, and varies in color from gray to brown. The branches grow horizontally from the trunk and are usually arranged in flattened sprays that curve downward at their tips. Short spur shoots, characteristic of many gymnosperms, are weakly to moderately developed in Tsuga. Young twigs and distal portions of the stem are flexible and often pendulous. The stems are rough due to the presence of pulvini, which persist after the leaves fall. Winter buds are ovoid or globose, rounded at the apex, and non-resinous. The leaves of Tsuga are flattened to slightly angular, measuring 5–35 mm in length and 1–3 mm in width. They are borne singly and arranged spirally along the stem, but the leaf bases are twisted, causing the leaves to lie flat on either side of the stem or, less commonly, radiate outward. The leaves narrow abruptly at the base into a petiole, which is set on a forward-angled pulvinus. The petiole is twisted at its base, aligning almost parallel to the stem. The leaf apex may be notched, rounded, or acute. The undersides of the leaves display two white stomatal bands separated by an elevated midvein, except in Tsuga mertensiana, where the bands are less conspicuous. The upper leaf surface lacks stomata, except in T. mertensiana. Each leaf contains a single resin canal located beneath the vascular bundle. The pollen cones of Tsuga are solitary, arising from lateral buds. They are small, measuring 3–5 mm in length (occasionally up to 10 mm), and vary in shape from ovoid to globose or ellipsoid. Their coloration ranges from yellowish-white to pale purple, and they are borne on short peduncles. The pollen grains have a saccate, ring-like structure at their distal pole, which may occasionally appear doubly saccate. The seed cones develop on year-old twigs and are small, ovoid-globose, or oblong-cylindrical, measuring 15–40 mm in length. In T. mertensiana, the cones are cylindrical and longer, ranging from 35–80 mm. The cones are solitary, terminal (rarely lateral), pendulous, and either sessile or borne on short peduncles up to 4 mm long. Cone maturation occurs within 5–8 months, after which the seeds are shed. The cones themselves are shed shortly after seed release or may persist for up to one or two years. The seed scales are thin, leathery, and persistent, lacking an apophysis or umbo. The bracts are small and included within the cone. The seeds are small, measuring 2–4 mm in length, with a wing 8–12 mm long. They contain small adaxial resin vesicles. Seed germination is epigeal, and the seedlings typically have four to six cotyledons. Tsuga mertensiana, or Mountain Hemlock, is unique within the genus. Its leaves are less flattened and arranged radially around the shoot, with stomata present on both the upper and lower surfaces, giving the foliage a glaucous appearance. Additionally, its cones are the longest in the genus, measuring 35–80 mm and cylindrical rather than ovoid. Some botanists classify this species in a separate genus, Hesperopeuce mertensiana, though it is more commonly treated as a subgenus. Another species, Bristlecone Hemlock (Tsuga longibracteata), is now placed in a distinct genus, Nothotsuga. This species differs from Tsuga in having erect cones with exserted bracts and male cones clustered in umbels, traits that align it more closely with the genus Keteleeria. Tsuga species are adapted to moist, cool temperate climates characterized by high rainfall, cool summers, and minimal water stress. They are well-suited to environments with heavy winter snowfall and are more tolerant of ice storms than most other tree species. The eastern North American species, Tsuga canadensis and Tsuga caroliniana, face significant threats from the sap-sucking insect Adelges tsugae, commonly known as the Hemlock Woolly Adelgid. This pest, introduced accidentally from eastern Asia, has caused extensive mortality, particularly in areas east of the Appalachian Mountains. Asian Tsuga species exhibit resistance to this pest, while the two western North American species show moderate resistance. Tsuga trees also serve as food sources for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species, including the Autumnal Moth and The Engrailed, as well as older caterpillars of the Gypsy Moth. The foliage of young trees is often browsed by deer, and the seeds are consumed by finches and small rodents. Older trees are susceptible to fungal diseases and decay caused by species such as Heterobasidion annosum and Armillaria, which rot the heartwood and increase susceptibility to windthrow. Rhizina undulata can kill groups of trees following minor grass fires, as the heat activates the growth of its spores. The wood of Tsuga species is highly valued in the timber industry, particularly for use as wood pulp. Many species are also cultivated for horticultural purposes, with numerous cultivars selected for use in gardens.
